sections.title: Square numbers and their properties
sections.body: A perfect square is any number you get by multiplying a natural number by itself — 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and so on are all perfect squares, since they equal 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5. One quick way to rule a number out is the unit's-digit test: every perfect square ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. A number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 can never be a perfect square — but the reverse isn't guaranteed: 26 ends in 6 yet isn't a perfect square, so passing this test only means 'maybe', never 'definitely yes'. A more powerful check is the odd-number-sum test: every perfect square n² is exactly the sum of the first n consecutive odd numbers starting from 1 — 1, 1+3=4, 1+3+5=9, 1+3+5+7=16, and so on. Equivalently, if you successively subtract 1, then 3, then 5, and so on from a number and land exactly on 0, that number is a perfect square; landing on a negative result partway through means it isn't. This same structure tells you how many non-square numbers sit between consecutive squares: between n² and (n+1)² there are always exactly 2n non-square numbers — for example, between 5²(=25) and 6²(=36) there are 2×5=10 non-square numbers. A separate, well-known pattern connects squares to right triangles: for any natural number m greater than 1, the three numbers 2m, m²−1 and m²+1 always form a Pythagorean triplet, meaning the squares of the two smaller numbers add up to the square of the largest. Not every Pythagorean triplet can be built this way, but this formula always produces a valid one.

sections.title: Finding square roots
sections.body: Finding a square root is the reverse of squaring: if y = x², then x is a square root of y. A perfect square strictly has two integer square roots, one positive and one negative (since (−x)² = x² too), but this course only ever uses the positive one, written with the symbol √. One way to find a square root by hand is repeated subtraction: keep subtracting consecutive odd numbers — 1, then 3, then 5, and so on — from the number, and if you land exactly on 0, the count of subtractions you made is the square root. This works but becomes slow for large numbers, so the more practical method is prime factorisation: break the number down into its prime factors, pair up identical factors, and multiply one factor from each pair together — that product is the square root. If even one prime factor is left without a partner, the number isn't a perfect square at all. This same idea tells you how to *fix* a near-miss: if a number's factorisation has one or more unpaired primes, multiplying by exactly those missing partners (or dividing them out) turns it into a perfect square — this is how you find the smallest number to multiply or divide by. For numbers that aren't perfect squares, you can still estimate the square root by bracketing: find the two consecutive whole numbers whose squares sit just below and just above the target, which pins the square root to that range, and you can narrow the range further by comparing to the midpoint's square. These methods aren't just abstract number theory — finding the side length of a square given its area, or applying the Pythagorean relation to find an unknown side of a right triangle, both come down to computing a square root.

sections.title: Cube numbers and their properties
sections.body: A perfect cube is a number you get by multiplying a natural number by itself three times — 1, 8, 27 and 64 are perfect cubes, since they equal 1×1×1, 2×2×2, 3×3×3 and 4×4×4. Checking whether a number is a perfect cube uses the same prime-factorisation idea as squares, but with triples instead of pairs: break the number into prime factors, and it's a perfect cube only if every single prime factor can be grouped into a complete set of exactly three. If any prime factor's count doesn't divide evenly into groups of three, the number isn't a perfect cube. That incomplete grouping also tells you exactly how to fix it: multiplying by the missing factor(s) completes the triple and produces a perfect cube, while dividing out the excess factor(s) that don't fit a triple does the same. A famous, purely numerical fact about cubes is the Hardy–Ramanujan number, 1729 — it's the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two genuinely different ways: 1³+12³ and 9³+10³ both equal 1729. It's a striking illustration that cube arithmetic can hide unexpected coincidences, discovered by the mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan.

sections.title: Finding cube roots
sections.body: Finding a cube root is the reverse of cubing: if y = x³, then x is the cube root of y, written with the symbol ∛. The most reliable hand method mirrors the square-root technique but works in threes instead of twos: break the number into its prime factors, group identical factors into complete triples, and multiply one factor from each triple together to get the cube root. This method extends naturally to real-world measurement problems — since the volume of a cube is (edge length)³, finding the edge length of a cube from its known volume is exactly the same calculation as finding a cube root by prime factorisation.

workedExamples.problem: Is 128 a perfect square? Use prime factorisation to justify your answer.
steps: Group the factors in pairs: 2⁷ = (2×2) × (2×2) × (2×2) × 2 — one factor of 2 is left unpaired.
Since not every prime factor pairs up, 128 is not a perfect square.
workedExamples.finalAnswer: No, 128 is not a perfect square — its prime factorisation leaves one 2 unpaired.

workedExamples.problem: A square plot of land has an area of 1,764 m². Find the length of one side.
steps: The side length is the square root of the area: side = √1764.
Pair the factors and multiply one from each pair: √1764 = 2 × 3 × 7 = 42.
workedExamples.finalAnswer: The side of the plot is 42 m.

workedExamples.problem: Find the smallest number by which 200 must be multiplied to make it a perfect cube.
steps: Group the factors in triples: 2³ is already a complete triple; 5² needs one more 5 to become 5³.
Multiply by the missing factor: 200 × 5 = 1000, which is 10³.

workedExamples.problem: Find the cube root of 5832 by prime factorisation.
steps: Group the factors in triples: 2³ is one triple; 3⁶ splits into two triples (3³ × 3³).
Multiply one factor from each triple: cube root = 2 × 3 × 3 = 18.

objectives.text: Identify a perfect square and use the unit's-digit rule to rule out non-squares.
Verify whether a number is a perfect square using the sum-of-consecutive-odd-numbers property.
Find the number of non-perfect-square numbers between two consecutive squares.
Construct a Pythagorean triplet using the 2m, m² − 1, m² + 1 form.
Find the square root of a perfect square by prime factorisation.
Find the square root of a perfect square by repeated subtraction of consecutive odd numbers.
Estimate the square root of a non-perfect-square number by bracketing between consecutive whole-number squares.
Find the smallest number by which a given number must be multiplied or divided to make it a perfect square, and apply this to real-world area/length problems.
Identify a perfect cube using prime factorisation (grouping factors in triples).
Find the smallest number by which a given number must be multiplied or divided to make it a perfect cube.
Find the cube root of a perfect cube by prime factorisation, including for real-world volume/edge-length problems.
